PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), pursuant to Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”) Rules of Practice and Procedure 212 and 213,1 
submits this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer to the comments and protests filed 
in response to PJM’s October 13, 2023 filing in this proceeding of proposed revisions to 
its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”)2 and Reliability Assurance Agreement 
(“RAA”) to enhance a number of facets of PJM’s capacity market (known as the Reliability 
Pricing Model (“RPM”).3  The capacity market enhancements proposed in both this 
proceeding and in Docket No. ER24-98-0004 significantly improve the market signals 
conveyed by the capacity market by better aligning the market representation of capacity 
supply and demand with expected resource performance and system resource adequacy 
risks.  Both filings are just and reasonable on a standalone basis, as explained and supported

I. 
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY 
In these proceedings, PJM proposed significant enhancements to its capacity 
market rules.  As PJM explained in the October 13 Filings, the energy transition and 
resulting changing resource mix in PJM is the primary driver of the need for the proposed 
capacity market enhancements.  The impetus for these changes is driven by the fact that 
resource retirements are currently outpacing replacement resources, leaving PJM at risk of 
a capacity shortfall by 2030 if changes are not made.5  While 2030 may seem far off, the 
forward nature of the capacity market means it is only a handful of Base Residual Auctions 
(“BRAs”) away.  PJM’s proposed enhancements will provide significant improvements to 
how PJM models and accredits resources and how resources are able to price risk in their 
offers.   
This answer and accompanying affidavits rebut material objections raised in the 
protests in this docket.  At the highest level, this answer addresses protests raised on various 
aspects of PJM’s proposal that include marginal accreditation, modelling assumptions used 
in both the ELCC analysis and reserve requirement study, resource performance 
adjustments in accreditation, generator testing requirements, and the annual stop-loss of 
Non-Performance Charges.  As further discussed in this answer and accompanying 
affidavits, such protests are without merit or do not rise to the level of rendering the

proposed design unjust and unreasonable.  Accordingly, the Commission has substantial 
evidence on which it can find the proposed changes to the Tariff and RAA to be just and 
reasonable.  The proposed changes to improve PJM’s existing modelling and accreditation 
processes are just and reasonable and address identified issues that will improve the 
reliability and efficiency benefits delivered by PJM’s capacity market.  But, these changes 
are not the end of the story.  PJM and many stakeholders recognize that potential 
enhancements beyond the contents of these filings warrant further exploration.  Topics of 
additional interest include exploring sub-annual market designs.  PJM remains committed 
to working with stakeholders to address the resource adequacy and other challenges 
stemming from the energy transition’s impact on the resource mix in the PJM Region.  This 
filing represents a significant step forward in evolving the PJM markets for the energy 
transition. Thus, the Commission should accept the reforms proposed in this proceeding.  
Furthermore, the Commission should resist calls for it to open a section 206 
proceeding into PJM’s capacity market and instead allow PJM and stakeholders to develop 
and consider potential further enhancements.6  PJM’s proposals enhance the current market 
rules, providing targeted and needed improvements.  Therefore, acceptance of the proposed 
enhancements in this filing effectively allows the Commission to simply deny as moot the 
pending complaint filed by the Independent Market Monitor for PJM (“Market Monitor”),7 
as it would establish a stop-loss that addresses the Market Monitor’s bankruptcy and 
liquidity concerns.

II. 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER 
Although Commission Rule 213(a)(2) does not generally permit answers to 
protests,8 the Commission permits answers for good cause shown, such as when an answer 
contributes to a more accurate and complete record or provides useful information that 
assists the Commission’s deliberative process.9  This answer will aid the Commission’s 
decision-making process by providing responses to the various comments and protests filed 
in response to the Reliability Enhancements Filing in this proceeding.  PJM therefore asks 
that the Commission accept this Answer. 
III. 
ANSWER 
A. 
The Proposed Marginal ELCC Accreditation Approach Is Just and 
Reasonable, Representing a Clear Enhancement Over the Status Quo. 
A diverse group of entities support PJM’s proposed marginal ELCC approach, 
including the Organization of PJM States, Inc.,10 two state commissions individually,11 the 
Pennsylvania Senate Energy Committee,12 industrial customers,13 and a wide array of 
generation interests.  Notably, the entities that support this proposal include those Market

The improvements that the marginal ELCC approach would bring are clear.

1. 
Marginal ELCC is a clear improvement over PJM’s current 
accreditation approaches. 
Currently, PJM uses the EFORd as a metric to accredit all generation resources, 
except solar, wind, storage, and hybrid resource types, which are accredited under an 
“average” ELCC approach.  The EFORd approach establishes the Unforced Capacity 
(“UCAP”) value of a resource as a function of the quantification of the average period of 
time a resource is on a forced outage.22  As a capacity accreditation approach, EFORd is 
fairly simplistic and only looks at the “resource’s service history in the twelve (12)

EFORd does not capture or reflect the common-mode failures that can drive resource 
adequacy risks (e.g., extreme weather or natural gas pipeline outages, where a common 
cause leads to multiple units going on outage concurrently, and at times, results in outage 
levels that are considerably higher than average) or how the reliability benefit of a given 
resource may vary with a changing load shape.  
While EFORd has been used to accredit the capacity value of most generation 
resources since the start of RPM, in 2021, PJM proposed and the Commission accepted the 
use of an average ELCC approach for accrediting wind, solar, storage, and hybrid Capacity 
Resources (known in the RAA as Variable Resources, Limited Duration Resources, and 
Combination Resources).  The Commission found PJM’s average approach, detailed in 
RAA, Schedule 9.1, just and reasonable because it: 
(1) reasonably assigns the same capacity value to resources with the same 
performance within a class, recognizing that all resources in a class contribute 
to changes to the overall ELCC of the class;  
(2) models all ELCC resources simultaneously, recognizing the possible 
synergistic and antagonistic interactions between resource classes, and ensures 
that the sum of resource classes’ accredited capacity values is equal to the 
aggregate reliability value of the ELCC Portfolio; and  
(3) informs ELCC Resources of their capacity accreditation prior to the capacity 
auction, which better informs resource entry and exit decisions.24 
The “marginal” ELCC approach proposed by PJM in this proceeding offers 
significant improvement in accrediting resources over EFORd and also improves upon the 
average ELCC approach.  Indeed, Dr. Rocha-Garrido explains that “marginal ELCC is

Resource’s expected marginal contribution to system resource adequacy based on the

In addition, as PJM has explained, the marginal ELCC approach improves on the 
existing approaches by:  
(1) accrediting at a higher proportion of installed capacity resources that provide 
higher marginal reliability benefit—thereby signaling investors to build more 
of this type of megawatts if cost-effective;  
(2) not assigning capacity capability to the proportion of installed capacity that risk 
modeling shows not likely to perform during [expected unserved energy 
(“EUE”)] events—thereby better ensuring the capacity committed, and for 
which load is paying, will actually show up when needed most; and  
(3) ensuring that each megawatt of capacity provides the same reliability value and 
therefore is substitutable one-for-one with other megawatts of PJM-accredited 
capacity.30 
Accordingly, the record demonstrates that marginal ELCC, combined with the updated risk 
modeling approach and adoption of the EUE metric keyed to the 1-in-10 loss of load 
expectation standard, will continue to allow PJM’s capacity market to send investment 
signals consistent with reliability needs.   
2. 
Challengers generally attack ex ante capacity accreditation 
determinations which are informative to entry/exit decisions. 
As detailed below, many objections to the marginal ELCC approach are really an 
attack on the underlying forward, annual capacity construct that PJM and other regions 
have long relied on to maintain resource adequacy.  Such philosophical challenges are not 
valid and in any event go beyond the scope of this section 205 filing in which PJM is not 
proposing to deviate from the current forward, annual capacity market structure.

the accreditation model, developed including information gathered through the Notice of 
Intent process that PJM is also proposing, is unlikely to be meaningfully different from the

In any event, PJM “re-accredits resources in updated versions of the annual

RPM was established in 2006.39  As such, the ex ante accreditation determination is not a 
change from the existing EFORd or average ELCC approaches, and thus, protestors’ 
challenges in this regard are arguably beyond the scope of this proceeding and should be

MARGINAL ACCREDITATION USING ENHANCED RISK MODEL  
II.A 
BASIS FOR COMPENSATION OF CAPACITY RESOURCES 
 The Independent Market Monitor (“IMM”) critiques the PJM proposal for 
compensating resources even when the resources are not available, arguing in 
favor of a purported alternative approach of “[p]aying resources only when they 
are available provides an important incentive to perform at all times. Paying 
resources only when they are available is a long term, predictable incentive for 
performance.”2 This argument reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of the role 
of accreditation in the capacity market.  
 In both the current and proposed market structures the capacity product is annual, 
with its value being assessed on that basis. Thus, PJM accredits resources annually 
and clears an annual market. PJM subsequently issues an annual payment 
reflecting resources’ accredited and cleared/committed quantity and the market 
value of that commitment. This directly reflects differences in accredited level 
across resources, thus making the annual payment reflect expected availability of 
capacity when it is most needed and providing no compensation for availability

compensated (say, in each hour) does not reflect the marginal value of that

considered reasonable so long as the payments corresponded to the marginal value 
of capacity at the time the resource is receiving payment. However, an annual 
capacity commitment period (and, indeed, even seasonal commitment periods in 
a more granular market) does not provide sufficiently granular prices to avoid the 
incentive issue raised above. Although it might be theoretically feasible to define 
accurate hourly capacity prices based on expected relative risks and hourly supply-
demand balance to mitigate this concern, it is at the moment impractical. To our 
knowledge, no other jurisdiction with a capacity market or resource adequacy 
framework has adopted this methodology. In the PJM proposal we instead adopt 
risk-weighted accreditation for an annual product, approaching the compensation 
outcomes under such a granular pricing and compensation design, augmented by 
high non-performance changes to increase the incentive for availability, and 
consequences of unavailability, during more risky operating periods.

II.C 
RELIABILITY IMPACT OF MARGINAL ELCC 
 The Public Interest Organizations (“PIOs”) argue that “Resource obligations under 
Marginal ELCC are insufficient to guarantee reliability” given PJM may “only 
procure UCAP equal to 97.2% of forecasted peak load” and “Suppliers’ 
obligations in RPM are based on their committed UCAP.” The PIOs further 
reference the New York Independent System Operator, Inc. (“NYISO”) market 
and recent filing to move to marginal accreditation, noting that “supplier 
obligations are expressed in ICAP in NYISO” and therefore “NYISO’s 
implementation of marginal ELCC are consistent with reliability.” 
 These arguments are without merit and factually incorrect (or incomplete at best). 
Today and under PJM’s proposal, there are a number of obligations placed on 
suppliers of committed capacity resources, some of which are based on the 
committed UCAP level, such as the Capacity Performance assessment during 
PAIs, while others are based on the committed ICAP level (or Installed Capacity 
equivalent of the committed UCAP), such as the energy market must offer 
obligation. Starting with the latter, under current and proposed rules, suppliers of 
committed generation capacity resources have an obligation under the Tariff to 
make their committed capacity available to PJM for scheduling by offering in the 
energy market, and such offers must be based on the “ICAP equivalent of the 
Market Seller’s cleared UCAP capacity commitment”10, after accounting for any 
unavailability due to being on outage at the time or other physical resource 
limitations. 
 For example, a 100 MW ICAP thermal generator that is accredited and committed 
for 80 MW UCAP is obligated to make available to PJM for scheduling the full 
100 MW of equivalent committed ICAP when not on outage; it is not limited to 
the 80 MW UCAP. If such a resource is on a full forced outage, the obligation and 
expectation is that the offer for such resource will be zero for the period of time 
that it is on outage, not the committed UCAP. Similarly, a committed solar 
capacity resource is obligated to offer and make available the forecasted level in 
each hour and not the accredited or committed UCAP in all hours. This would be 
zero at night (similar to a thermal generator on outage), and generally greater than 
the committed UCAP during the midday hours. 
 In this way, the energy market must offer obligation represents the physical 
amount of committed capacity suppliers must make available to PJM throughout 
all hours of the year, recognizing that the level of physical capacity available at 
any particular time will naturally vary, as resources go on forced or planned 
outages, or are otherwise not available such as solar at night. This is entirely 
consistent with the underlying hourly representations of such committed capacity

classes of potential approaches, statistical and structural.

minimum temperatures, and even more extreme temperatures risk under-stating 
the prevalence of extreme winter weather and entirely eliminating any indication 
that the coldest weather historically observed may, in fact, reoccur with some

“stronger” trend in minimum annual temperatures identified by Mr. Wilson of

III.A CHANGE TO CAPACITY PERFORMANCE PENALTY STOP-LOSS 
 While certain parties have filed in support of the proposed change to index the 
annual stop-loss of Non-Performance Charges to the Base Residual Auction 
(“BRA”) clearing price rather than Net CONE, others have protested and argued, 
among other things, that this change will undermine resource performance 
incentives and degrade reliability, and will add further uncertainty to the 
development of offers, particularly with respect to CP risk. 
 After careful consideration of the protests, we continue to find the proposed stop-
loss, set at 1.5 times the BRA clearing price, to be just and reasonable. 
Fundamentally, the stop-loss is intended to bound a market seller’s exposure to 
non-performance risk of a committed resource in a year, and seeks to strike a 
balance between being sufficiently high to maintain performance incentives and 
low enough to avoid excessive risk exposure. There is no single correct answer to 
where this balance should fall, but we believe the PJM proposal improves that 
balance relative to status quo by: (1) lowering the stop-loss in years with relatively 
low clearing prices as recently observed, thereby reducing the tail risk sellers can 
face today where annual non-performance charges can be many times greater than 
annual capacity revenues; and (2) keeping the stop-loss sufficiently high in any 
one year such that a seller is exposed to lose more than the capacity revenues they 
earn from clearing in the auction.  
 Constellation and others argue that the proposal will harm reliability when the 
market clears low, as it provides a relatively low number of PAIs for which a non-
performing resource will be exposed, and therefore reduces incentives for 
investment and performance. By way of example, Constellation notes that PJM’s 
proposal would result in the stop-loss limit being reached in just 4.4 hours (when 
using the 24/25 BRA RTO prices and assuming a unit provides zero performance 
during the PAIs and the balancing ratios are 1), or 8.6 hours (when using the 22/23 
BRA RTO price – the year of Winter Storm Elliott).  
 Having a relatively low number of hours in which the stop-loss could be reached 
does not in and of itself make the proposed change unreasonable. By definition, 
any stop-loss provides a point at which a resource is no longer exposed to Non-
Performance Charges. The key question, in striking the appropriate balance, is if 
the potential Non-Performance Charges collected over those hours provide 
appropriately strong incentives for the resource to invest in reliability-improving 
measures and perform when needed. The proposed stop-loss does this by not only

[Page 79]
subjecting a resource to the loss of 100% of their annual capacity revenues, but 
further exposes the resource to a net loss of up to 50% of the annual revenues. This 
exposure to lose significantly more than the annual capacity revenues provides an 
appropriately strong signal for investment and performance. 
 Furthermore, even once an under-performing resource has reached its stop-loss, 
there continues to be reasonably strong incentives to perform from both the energy 
and capacity market compensation beyond exposure to penalties during PAIs. 
First, energy market prices will tend to be high during PAIs, particularly under the 
recently revised Emergency Action definition that considers reserve shortage 
periods. Second, the stop-loss is assessed against gross non-performance charges, 
and Capacity Market Sellers of Capacity Resources that hit their stop-loss are still 
eligible and incentivized to receive capacity bonus payments for performance

accreditation provide a stronger incentive to perform than in the past, as any 
continued failure to perform (thereby remaining on outage) can significantly 
impact the modeled availability of the resource in the ELCC analysis, particularly 
when those failures are during times of system reliability risk, such that a non-
performing resource is incentivized to come back from an outage as soon as 
possible to avoid further lowering its accredited capacity value and capacity 
revenue stream for the future. 
 It is also worth noting in response to these arguments, and in recognition that there 
is more than one reasonable approach to this construct, that the rules approved by 
the Commission in ISO-NE have a non-performance charge rate that is higher than

MARKET POWER MITIGATION AND MARKET SELLER OFFER CAP  
A 
ASSESSMENT OF CPQR UNDER UNKNOWN STOP-LOSS 
 Intervenors raised issues regarding market sellers’ abilities to assess CPQR, and 
therefore their competitive offer, before the stop-loss is known. We have reviewed 
the issues and find the arguments unconvincing. 
 First, the specific stop-loss level is but one variable among many that market 
sellers must estimate when developing a cost-reflective competitive offer. Such 
unknowns include actual delivery year net energy and ancillary services market 
revenue (which itself depends on actual operations, fuel costs, and E&AS market 
prices); costs of any investments and fixed O&M costs that are required to remain 
operational; and CP-related potential bonus or penalty payments, themselves 
dependent on other unknowns including the number of PAIs, resources 
performance during PAIs, the balancing ratio, and other unknowns. In other words, 
as in any forward market, the actual costs of satisfying the forward commitment 
depend on conditions at and around the time the commitment must be satisfied 
that are as of yet unknown when the forward offer is made. Assumptions are 
inherent in a forward market.  
 Indeed, in the context of the other unknowns that must be estimated in the process 
of constructing an offer, the exact stop loss should be expected to have 
substantially less of an impact on resources’ competitive offer level than many of 
these other variables. Indeed, uncertainty over the level of the stop loss only rarely 
affects participants’ incurred penalties, when at least: (1) there are sufficient PAIs 
such that any resource would reach the stop loss; and (2) a given resources’ 
performance is sufficiently poor such during those PAIs that the stop loss is 
reached. In other words, reaching the stop-loss is itself a tail-probability event, and 
thus the impacts of changes must be discounted.  
 Further, certain of these other unknowns also vary directly as a result of capacity 
auction outcomes. For example, the probability of experiencing PAIs and the

[Page 87]
number of PAIs change depending on whether the capacity auction clears a high 
reserve margin compared to a low one. Thus, fixing the stop loss level before the 
auction would not allow market participants to avoid assessing potential market 
clearing outcomes when developing their competitive offers, if reducing such 
dependence were even a design consideration.

RELIABILITY BENEFITS AND EFFICIENCY BENEFITS IN CONTEXT 
 In response to the auction clearing and reliability analysis previously presented in 
the Graf Affidavit, the IMM argues that “PJM claimed that this 25% increase in

 This perspective is flawed because it focuses on the increase in customer costs 
rather that fairly attempting to understand the overall impacts on a more holistic 
metric of market efficiency. It is essential to consider the bigger picture of overall 
welfare, including both consumer surplus and producer surplus. Consumer surplus 
refers to the value consumers receive, net of the costs they incur. Producer surplus 
represents the revenues producers earn, net of their production costs. 
 From this broader viewpoint, it becomes clear that the change in customer costs 
largely corresponds to an increase in supplier net profits rather than a true societal 
cost. Such a redistribution does not inherently imply a decrease in societal welfare. 
In fact, when assessing the overall efficiency of the system, a more appropriate 
measure is the total decrease in system-wide supply costs. In the case of the 
analysis in question previously presented in the Graf Affidavit, there is a notable 
5% reduction in the overall costs of supply, corresponding to a $20 million 
decrease in the total offered costs of cleared resources. This decrease is significant 
and should not be overlooked. It reflects a more efficient allocation of resources 
within the market, leading to cost savings at a systemic level. We find similar 
results in the updated analysis discussed above. 
 While the per-MWh customer cost increase seems substantial when viewed in 
isolation, it is a limited perspective that does not capture the full economic picture. 
When considering the decrease in overall supply costs and the added value of 
increased reliability, the changes proposed by PJM represent a clear win in terms 
of overall societal welfare and efficiency.

Using the ELCC/RRS run that meets the 1-day-in-10-years reliability criteria,

planned/maintenance outage rate (explained below) in the corresponding 
hour on all days in the bin since June 1st, 2012. The result of the addition 
constitutes the total outage rate. For example, if bin B includes days D, D1, 
D2, D3, then add up the historical forced outage F of the resource, the

The modeled planned/maintenance outage rate for a resource in an hour with loss of load 
is calculated as follows: 
- 
Identify the total megawatt amount of planned and maintenance outages in 
the hour with loss of load; 
- 
For the resource, identify the annual planned/maintenance outage 
requirement in megawatts-weeks; 
- 
For the entire set of resources, calculate the annual planned/maintenance 
outage requirement in megawatts-weeks; 
- 
For the resource, estimate the share of annual planned/maintenance outage 
requirement relative to the annual planned/maintenance outage requirement 
for the entire set of resources; and

Multiply the resource’s share of planned/maintenance outage requirement 
by the total megawatt amount of planned and maintenance outages in the 
hour with loss of load. This result divided by the ICAP of the resource is 
the modeled planned/maintenance outage rate for a resource in an hour with 
loss of load.

The proposed ELCC/RRS model includes assumptions around the dispatch of Limited 
Duration and Demand Resources that do not involve a full unit commitment and dispatch 
as the IMM correctly points out. PJM is open to consider such dispatch option in the future. 
Such dispatch options, however, would require an important number of assumptions that 
would need to be carefully worked through. 
34. 
The IMM also claims that events like Winter Storm Elliott are not captured in the proposed 
ELCC/RRS model.33 This claim is not correct. The level of thermal forced outages during 
Winter Storm Elliott, the load levels the system experienced and the correlation between 
the cold temperatures and levels of unavailability experience by the overall PJM fleet are 
all included in the model.  
35. 
The IMM also questions using the concept of a Solved Load in the Reserve Requirement 
Study.34 The need for the concept of the Solved Load arises because the amount of 
resources that historically have been expected to offer and clear in RPM exceeds the 
amount needed to meet the 1-day-in-10-years reliability criteria. Therefore, calculating the 
loss of load expectation of such resource mix relative to the forecasted loads and associated 
load uncertainty for a future year, requires to iteratively adjust either the load shapes up or 
the supply shapes down until achieving an LOLE equal to 0.1 days/year (because the 
starting LOLE will be lower than 0.1 days/year). PJM has historically chosen to iteratively 
adjust the load shapes up given that it is less arbitrary than removing resources from the 
supply side. Because the hourly load shapes are iteratively adjusted in tandem, maintaining 
the relationship between the loads (e.g., if an extreme load is 107% of the median load in 
the original load shape, then after the adjustment to find the Solved Load, the extreme load 
will still be 107% of the median load, even if the megawatt load values are different in the 
adjusted shape relative to the original load shape), the magnitude of the load uncertainty 
relative to the median peak load is preserved. The main objective of the RRS is to determine 
the level of UCAP (i.e., the FPR), expressed as a percent of the Solved Load required to 
meet the reliability criteria. This level of UCAP is mainly driven by load uncertainty. For 
example, an FPR equal to 1.05 means that the system needs 5% of UCAP reserves in excess 
of the median peak load because of load uncertainty. As noted earlier, proportionally, load 
uncertainty does not change after adjusting the loads by the Solved Load. Therefore, 
applying an FPR calculated using the Solved Load to the forecasted median peak load is 
appropriate.
